John Cabot was a Venetian-born explorer who sailed under the English flag to explore the North American coast in 1497, establishing England's claim to portions of the continent. Though his expedition lasted only a few weeks and his precise landing site remains uncertain, his voyage created the foundation for British colonial expansion in North America centuries later.

He sailed westward from Bristol in 1497 under the sponsorship of King Henry VII, five years after Columbus. His ship, the Matthew, carried a crew of only about eighteen men and was vastly smaller than Columbus's fleet. He reached land somewhere along the North American coast—likely Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, or Maine—though contemporary accounts are vague and historians still dispute his exact landfall.

When he returned to England, he claimed to have discovered a new continent and believed he had reached Asia, the most northern part of the world. King Henry VII gave him ten pounds upon his return and promised future support. His second expedition in 1498 never returned, and the details of his fate remain unclear. Yet his voyage gave England a claim to explore and eventually settle North America, a claim used centuries later to justify English colonization. Descendants of his name, the Cabots, were later prominent in exploring and claiming territories for the English crown.
